title: Lay-led communities
hook: independent minyanim, where members lead prayer themselves

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: no label needed. Some Jews choose no movement at all and simply describe what they do. Could you say your own practice in one plain sentence? Today, communities that run themselves. Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.

A woman in a sweater gets up from a folding chair, walks to the front of a rented room above a bookshop, and begins the morning prayers. Behind her, a borrowed Torah scroll waits in a cabinet, beside a box of prayer books someone carried up the stairs. There is no rabbi on a stage, because there is no stage. Later a teenager reads from the Torah, nervous, carefully prepared. A retired dentist gives a five-minute thought on the week's portion. Next week, three different people will do those jobs. Groups like this go by a plain name: an independent minyan. They are today's word.
screen: `A WOMAN IN A SWEATER LEADS.` → `NO STAGE, NO PULPIT.` → `MEMBERS TAKE TURNS.`

segments.voice: Lay-led communities. Turn it four ways. First, the quorum. A minyan is the group Jewish law asks for when a community prays together; the Mishnah lists prayers that are not said with fewer than ten. Streams differ on who counts toward the ten. What the law asks for is people, not a building and not a title. Second, the leader is a role, not a rank. The person who leads the prayers is called the shaliach tzibbur, the messenger of the congregation. Jewish law does not require a rabbi for that job. Any member who knows the prayers can stand up and carry the room's words for a while, then sit back down. Third, the old picture behind it. At Sinai, the Torah says, God told the whole people: "ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation." Readers have heard many things in that line. Some members of lay-led groups hear a job description: the holiness belongs to everyone in the room, so the work can too. Fourth, the cost. Nobody is paid to do it, so somebody has to. Someone sets up the chairs. Someone learns to chant a Torah portion. Someone brings the food, and someone stays to wash the cups. Independent minyanim vary a great deal: some are egalitarian, some keep traditional practice, some sit between. Some members also belong to a synagogue with a rabbi, and value both. What they share is the habit of handing the work around. A room like that only exists because ordinary people decided to lead it.
screen: `THE LAW ASKS FOR PEOPLE.` · `A MESSENGER, NOT A RANK.` · `A KINGDOM OF PRIESTS.` · `SOMEONE SETS UP THE CHAIRS.` · then, large: `LAY-LED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lead one small thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of a group you already belong to: a household, a team, a group chat, a few friends. Find one small job in it that usually waits for someone else. Starting the meal. Picking the song. Setting the table. Opening the conversation that keeps getting postponed. Picture yourself doing it today, simply, without making it a speech. If you pray, you can offer the job up as you breathe. If you don't, just hold the picture steady. The bell holds the time.
Lay-led communities. Groups where members, not paid clergy, lead prayer, read Torah and teach, taking turns as the messenger of the congregation. Today's word.
Your line: lay-led. Today, step forward for one small job in a group you belong to, the one nobody has picked up yet. Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: In independent minyanim, members take turns leading prayer, reading from the Torah and giving short teachings, and members share the practical work of setting up, hosting and cleaning up.
